{{Short description|Mathematical conjecture}}

{{Expert needed|1=Mathematics|date=January 2024}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Conley conjecture''', named after mathematician [[Charles C. Conley|Charles Conley]], is a conjecture in the field of [[symplectic geometry]], a branch of [[differential geometry]].

==Background==

Let <math>(M, \omega)</math> be a compact [[symplectic manifold]]. A [[vector field]] <math>V</math> on <math>M</math> is called a  [[Hamiltonian vector field]] if the 1-form <math>\omega( V, \cdot)</math> is exact (i.e., equals to the differential of a function <math>H</math>. A Hamiltonian diffeomorphism <math>\phi: M \to M</math> is the integration of a 1-parameter family of Hamiltonian vector fields <math>V_t, t \in [0, 1]</math>.

In [[dynamical system]]s, one would like to understand the distribution of fixed points or periodic points. A periodic point of a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism <math>\phi</math> (of period <math>k</math>) is a point <math>x \in M</math> such that <math>\phi^k(x) = x </math>. A feature of Hamiltonian dynamics is that Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms tend to have infinitely many periodic points. [[Conley]] first made such a conjecture for the case that <math>M</math> is a torus.{{refn|Charles Conley, Lecture at University of Wisconsin, April 6, 1984. <ref name =GinzburgGürel2015>{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/s40598-015-0017-3 |title=The Conley Conjecture and Beyond |date=2015 |last1=Ginzburg |first1=Viktor L. |last2=Gürel |first2=Başak Z. |journal=Arnold Mathematical Journal |volume=1 |issue=3 |pages=299–337 |s2cid=256398699 |doi-access=free |arxiv=1411.7723 |bibcode=2015ArnMJ...1..299G }}</ref>}}

The Conley conjecture is false in many simple cases. For example, a rotation of a round sphere <math>S^2</math> by an angle equal to an [[irrational number|irrational]] multiple of <math>\pi</math>, which is a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism, has only 2 geometrically different periodic points.{{R|GinzburgGürel2015}} On the other hand, it has been [[mathematical proof|proved]] for various types of symplectic manifolds.

==History of studies==

The Conley conjecture was proved by Franks and Handel for surfaces with positive genus.<ref>{{cite journal |url=http://eudml.org/doc/123400 |title=Periodic points of Hamiltonian surface diffeomorphisms |journal=Geometry & Topology |date=2003 |volume=7 |pages=713–756 |last1=Franks |first1=John |last2=Handel |first2=Michael |issue=2 |doi=10.2140/gt.2003.7.713 |s2cid=2140632 |doi-access=free |arxiv=math/0303296 }}</ref> The case of higher dimensional torus was proved by Hingston.<ref>{{cite journal 
|doi=10.4007/annals.2009.170.529|title=Subharmonic solutions of Hamiltonian equations on tori |date=2009 |last1=Hingston |first1=Nancy |journal=Annals of Mathematics |volume=170 |issue=2 |pages=529–560 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Hingston's proof inspired the proof of [[Viktor Ginzburg|Ginzburg]] of the Conley conjecture for symplectically aspherical manifolds. Later, Ginzburg--Gurel and Hein proved the Conley conjecture for manifolds whose first Chern class vanishes on spherical classes. Finally, Ginzburg--Gurel proved the Conley conjecture for negatively monotone symplectic manifolds.
